newsitem.title: UK: Short stg predicts more UK rate rises post-budget.
newsitem.headline: Short stg predicts more UK rate rises post-budget.

text.p: British interest rate futures fell on Wednesday as the fiscal tightening in Chancellor Gordon Brown's inaugural budget failed to relieve the perceived need for further interest rate rises, analysts said.

"Short sterling's been sold off, I guess that's because the market's come to the conclusion that a tight budget's not going to stop rates from going up," said Marian Bell, treasury market economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland.
Analysts said the new, slightly higher market predictions for interest rates going into next year were now more realistic.
"We think the market is close to fair value now," said Tom Rayner, gilts analyst at Societe Generale in London.

Short sterling managed to inch ahead initially across the strip as Brown said he would tighten fiscal policy by 5.5 billion sterling this year, more than the four billion the market had been looking for.
But the contracts soon lost ground as analysts delved into the details of the fiscal tightening and expressed concern at consumer spending, seen up by 4.5 percent this year and 4.0 percent in 1998.

"The feeling seems to be that it (the budget) doesn't seem to be so tight, basically," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. "The numbers seem to be tight but given the details it doesn't seem as fearsome as predicted."

By 1625 GMT, December short sterling was down 14 basis points at 92.63 in automated trade, off its earlier high of 92.84. This implies official rates of around 7.25 percent by the end of the year, from their current 6.5 percent.
March 1998 short sterling was also down 14 basis points at 92.55, off 92.76 earlier, and the June 1998 contract was down 13 basis points at 92.54.
Rayner said the market may come down even further after the dust has settled on the budget, and he added he did not foresee any significant rally.
Brown always faced a dilemma in his maiden budget as the need to curb consumer spending conflicted with pre-election promises not to raise income taxes, analysts said.
The Bank of England said the budget helped to tackle the UK policy dilemma.
"The Bank welcomes the budget. It certainly helps to address the policy dilemma we are confronted with," a central bank official said.
The central bank's interest rate setting monetary policy committee is due to meet next week with a decision on rates due to be announced on July 10.
